subject: Agriculture
title: Pakistan's Wheat Boom
description: A quick, practical guide to Pakistan's Wheat Boom.

hook.text: In 1967, Pakistan planted Borlaug's Mexican wheat on a massive scale. The harvest was staggering.

buildup.text: The government imported 42,000 tons of seed—the largest seed purchase in history at that time.

discovery.text: Pakistan's wheat production nearly doubled between 1965 and 1970. The country achieved food self-sufficiency.

twist.text: Success depended on tube wells for irrigation. Farmers with wells prospered; those without fell further behind.

climax.text: The Green Revolution worked in Pakistan—but unevenly. Wealth flowed to those who could afford the inputs.

punchline.text: The miracle seeds needed miracle access. Not everyone had it.

quiz.question: How much seed did Pakistan import for its Green Revolution wheat program?

details.summary: Pakistan adopted Green Revolution wheat varieties in the late 1960s and nearly doubled its wheat production within five years. This topic covers how Pakistan's wheat boom paralleled India's, the role of government policy in diffusing the technology, and the uneven distribution of benefits.

takeaways: Pakistan's wheat production nearly doubled between 1965 and 1970 with new varieties
Government subsidies for fertilizer, irrigation, and seed accelerated adoption rapidly
Benefits disproportionately favored larger farmers with access to irrigation and credit

faq.question: How quickly did Pakistan adopt Green Revolution wheat?
faq.answer: Pakistan imported Mexican semi-dwarf wheat in 1965. By 1970, the new varieties covered over 50% of wheat area. Production jumped from 3.4 million tons to 6.7 million tons in just five years. Government subsidies for inputs and guaranteed purchase prices drove rapid farmer adoption.

faq.question: Why did Pakistan's wheat boom benefit some farmers more than others?
faq.answer: Green Revolution varieties required irrigation, purchased fertilizer, and credit for seeds—resources available mainly to larger, wealthier landowners. Smallholders and rain-fed farmers were left behind. The technology gap increased rural inequality even as total food production soared.
